tldr: A mobile bimanual robot capable of high-DOF whole-body coordination—which typically costs over $70k–$100k commercially—was realized as an open-source platform with a parts cost of about $8.1k (around 1.2 million JPY). It seamlessly connects intuitive whole-body teleoperation via Apple Vision Pro to policy learning and real-robot deployment using imitation learning (ACT) through a unified control pipeline.
hero_caption: Physical appearance of MABEL, the developed life-sized mobile bimanual robot. Despite featuring 56 DOFs (59 motors), it achieves both rich functionality and an astonishingly low parts cost of about $8,056.
overview:
As robot learning expands from tabletop setups to entire household environments, mobile base locomotion, height adjustment, active visual exploration via neck articulation, and dexterous bimanual, multi-fingered manipulation have become indispensable. However, commercial humanoids and research platforms offering all these features are extremely expensive, costing $69k to $120k or more. Meanwhile, affordable open-source alternatives are limited to hobby servos, 1-DOF grippers, and fixed vertical columns, and combining custom parts costs researchers enormous software integration effort.

To bridge this gap, the research team developed MABEL, a fully integrated open-source robot spanning hardware, control, teleoperation, simulation, and learning pipelines. MABEL features an omnidirectional 3-wheel swerve base, a vertical lift, a pitching torso, two back-drivable 7-DOF arms, 17-DOF multi-fingered hands, and a 3-DOF active neck, all built with a parts cost of just around $8,056 (approx. 1.2 million JPY).

Furthermore, leveraging the Apple Vision Pro, they built an intuitive whole-body teleoperation system that retargets sparse tracking of the head and hands directly into whole-body motions without handheld controllers. The robot's visual feed reaches the headset with an ultra-low latency of just 137 ms.

Real-robot evaluations confirmed a median positional repeatability of 1.65 mm and high omnidirectional base accuracy both indoors and outdoors. Teleoperation succeeded in diverse household tasks, such as accessing a dishwasher and retrieving items from high shelves. In addition, using data collected via teleoperation, an autonomous pick-and-place task was trained and deployed using Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), demonstrating the practical utility of the end-to-end pipeline.
contributions: Provision of a fully open-source hardware platform with 56-DOF whole-body coordination (omnidirectional base, lift, pitching torso, back-drivable bimanual arms, 17-DOF multi-fingered hands, and 3-DOF active neck) for a parts cost of roughly $8.1k.

Construction of a low-latency, controller-free whole-body teleoperation interface that intuitively drives the entire body (base, lift, torso, neck, arms, multi-fingered hands) from sparse Vision Pro head and hand tracking.

Establishment of an integrated learning pipeline sharing the exact same command interface and compliant whole-body controller across teleoperation, simulation, data collection, and policy deployment, demonstrated end-to-end with an ACT policy.

sections.heading: Why do we now need an affordable, full-body open robot?
sections.summary: While advances in imitation learning push robots toward complex household tasks, prohibitively expensive hardware remains a major bottleneck. MABEL offers a fully open-source solution that delivers whole-body motion, active perception, and compliant physical interaction at one-tenth the cost of commercial alternatives, complete with an integrated learning pipeline.
sections.details:
The frontier of robot learning is no longer confined to the tabletop. It demands broad reach from floor level to high shelves, mobility across rooms, active perception to point cameras where needed, and compliant bimanual, multi-fingered manipulation with physical contact. However, commercial robots offering these capabilities are exceedingly expensive, running from $69,000 to over $120,000. Constrained by budget, many labs rely on low-cost hobby-servo robots or exhaust themselves piecing together disparate commercial parts and writing custom software.

MABEL (Mobile Anthropomorphic Bimanual Embodiment for Learning) was created to close this gap. At a parts cost of $8,056, it delivers reach from the floor up to 2.23 m, quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators in the torso and arms that yield compliantly to external forces, a holonomic mobile base, an active neck, and 17-DOF multi-fingered hands.

In addition, by simply wearing an Apple Vision Pro, an operator can control the robot's entire body as if inhabiting its physical frame. Because simulation, teleoperation, and trained policy execution all share the same controller, collected demonstration data can feed directly into policy learning without friction.

captions.F2: Comparison of MABEL's workspace and camera coverage. (a) Broad fingertip workspace reaching from the floor to 2.23 m via lift and torso pitch, (b) visual field expanded to roughly triple that of a torso-fixed camera through neck and torso motion, and (c) vertical reach compared against prior open-source robots and human baselines.

sections.heading: Where prior platforms fall short and how MABEL breaks through
sections.summary: Existing low-cost platforms trade off arm degrees of freedom, reach, or contact compliance, and their teleoperation setups often separate base and gaze control. MABEL unifies all these capabilities, achieving commercial-grade embodiment at an order of magnitude lower cost.
sections.details:
Recent years have seen numerous low-cost robot platforms emerge. Notable pioneers include ALOHA, which popularized low-cost teleoperation, and Mobile ALOHA, which added mobility. However, these rely on position-controlled servos with a small 0.75 kg payload, and their workspace is largely restricted to table height.

Sub-$1,000 platforms like XLeRobot compromise on reach and degrees of freedom. Systems with vertical lifts such as TidyBot++ or YOR keep cameras fixed or restrict end-effectors to 1-DOF parallel grippers. While commercial platforms integrate these capabilities, prices well above $70,000 and months of downtime for repairs hinder research velocity.

Teleoperation interfaces have also suffered from fragmentation, typically separating master-slave arm rigs from pedal- or joystick-controlled mobile bases and lifts. Even with the recent rise of VR headsets, many setups track only the upper body. By aligning its design and algorithms with human proportions, MABEL enables an operator to steer the base, lift, torso, neck, arms, and fingers as a single unified body using only headset and hand tracking.

sections.heading: The secret behind achieving 56 DOFs for around $8,100
sections.summary: MABEL cleverly combines a 3-wheel swerve base, a commercial standing-desk lift column, an adapted open-source OpenArm, 17-DOF ORCA hands, and a 3-DOF neck. Blending off-the-shelf parts, 3D printing, and custom PCBs, a complete unit can be assembled and verified in just two weeks.
sections.details:
### III-A Mechanical Design (Mobility, Arms, Torso)
For the mobile base, three battle-tested REV MAXSwerve modules from competitive robotics are used. Arranging three modules in a non-collinear layout rather than the standard four wheels eliminates wheel hop on uneven ground while cutting roughly $700 in cost. The tipping risk caused by a smaller support polygon is safely managed by the center-of-mass controller described later.

The arms consist of two 7-DOF manipulators based on the open-source OpenArm, built for roughly $3,000 for both arms via direct sourcing. The torso integrates a quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuator providing $-60^\circ$ to $15^\circ$ pitch bending, combined with an off-the-shelf standing-desk electric lift column to achieve reaching heights from floor level up to 2.23 m. A 3-DOF neck roughly triples visual coverage compared to a torso-fixed camera. The wrists are modular, allowing quick swaps between 17-DOF tendon-driven ORCA hands and parallel grippers.

### III-B Electronics, Sensors, and Compute
Power distribution and communication are handled by a custom Teensy-based PCB. The mobile base and upper body run on separate CAN buses and communicate with the host PC over Ethernet, ensuring bandwidth and reliability. Supported host computers include the Raspberry Pi 5, Jetson Orin/Thor, and MacBook. A 24 V onboard battery provides roughly 4 hours of runtime, with support for power-tool batteries or continuous AC wall power. The head mounts a stereo camera (ZED Mini), and both wrists feature RGB cameras (RealSense D405).

### III-C Fabrication and Reproducibility
MABEL is constructed from commercial off-the-shelf parts, laser-cut sheet metal, and 3D-printed components, bringing total parts cost to $8,056 with a Raspberry Pi 5. Using the released design files and BOM, building and verifying a second physical robot took approximately two weeks, proving high reproducibility.

captions.F4: Cutaway view of MABEL's internal packaging. Motors (yellow), structural components (gray), sensors (orange), electronics and PCBs (purple), and battery (green) are color-coded by function, illustrating compact, high-density integration.

sections.heading: Full-body control from Vision Pro alone: intuitive teleoperation and control
sections.summary: A retargeting approach maps sparse Apple Vision Pro tracking (head and hands only) onto 56 robot DOFs without ambiguity. It incorporates dynamic anti-tip limits for the swerve base and impedance control that yields compliantly to external contact.
sections.details:
### IV-A Interface and Communication
Operation is completely controller-free, relying solely on Apple Vision Pro head pose and hand/fingertip keypoint tracking. The operator sees real-scale stereo imagery streamed from the robot's head cameras; matching human interpupillary distance (approx. 63 mm) yields highly natural depth perception. Video and control packets stream over the robot's Wi-Fi hotspot to minimize latency.

### IV-B Sparse Tracking to Whole-Body Retargeting
Because Vision Pro tracks only the head, wrists, and fingertips, driving 56 DOFs is an underdetermined problem. After an initial ~10-second calibration to estimate the operator's proportions, motion is cleanly decoupled:

- **Torso and Locomotion**: The operator's head displacement is evaluated against a "comfort box." Small forward or lateral leans map to torso pitch bending; larger excursions beyond the box are treated as walking intent and mapped to base planar translation. Vertical head motion directly commands the lift column.
- **Neck and Arms**: The 3-DOF neck mirrors the head orientation relative to the torso. Arm motions scale wrist positions relative to the shoulders by bodily proportions, solved via damped Gauss-Newton inverse kinematics (IK) into smooth joint trajectories.
- **Hands**: For the 17-DOF ORCA hands, fingertip positioning is augmented with a penalty weight $w_{\mathrm{pinch}}$ on thumb-to-fingertip relative vectors, preserving precise grasp apertures during pinching motions.

### IV-C Tip-Over Aware Base Kinematics
While the 3-wheel swerve base is compact, extending the lift elevates the center of mass, raising tip-over risks. Based on zero-moment point (ZMP) principles, a height-aware velocity and acceleration limiter dynamically constrains allowable accelerations based on lift height $z_{\mathrm{lift}}$, preventing rollovers during sharp turns or abrupt stops.

### IV-D Whole-Body Compliant Control
The arms and torso employ joint-space impedance control. Because gravity compensation $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{g}}$ and friction compensation $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{f}}$ are accurately modeled, stiffness gains can remain low, allowing compliant behavior where external contact from human hands gently pushes the arms or torso aside.

(a) Coordinate frame correspondence and whole-body mapping between human and robot, (b) virtual joystick enabling foot-free navigation in confined rooms, and (c) first-person and third-person immersive teleoperation views seen by the operator.

sections.heading: An integrated software pipeline from data collection to policy deployment
sections.summary: A unified control pipeline bridges simulation environments (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) and the physical hardware. Demonstrations collected via teleoperation are stored in LeRobot format, allowing straightforward imitation learning (ACT) training and deployment.
sections.details:
### V-A Simulation Environments (Digital Twins)
Full-body simulation assets spanning all 59 actuated joints are provided for MuJoCo and Isaac Lab, alongside 35 static and dynamic evaluation scenes. Because simulation and physical hardware share the exact same hardware abstraction layer (HAL) and command interfaces, controllers and learned policies developed in simulation transfer to the physical robot without code changes.

### V-B Data Collection and Format
During Vision Pro teleoperation, the robot logs the 59-dimensional whole-body state $\boldsymbol{\mathbf{q}}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{59}$, covering arms (14 joints), hands (34 joints), neck (3 joints), torso pitch, lift, and swerve base. Synchronized 30 Hz RGB streams from the head stereo and wrist cameras, timestamped joint commands, and base velocities are recorded and exported to the standard LeRobot v3 format.

### V-C Robot Learning Model (ACT)
Demonstration datasets train Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policies. The model encodes head and wrist camera images alongside joint histories from the past 1 second, using a transformer to predict a future chunk of joint targets (chunk $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{q}}}^*$ over $K=120$ steps, approx. 4 seconds). These predicted trajectories are executed safely on the real robot through the identical whole-body controller used during teleoperation.

captions.F7: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) training and deployment pipeline. Taking head and wrist camera images and past joint states as input, the policy predicts a chunk of future joint targets across all 59 body coordinates to drive the physical robot.

sections.heading: Rigorous real-robot benchmarks: accuracy, latency, chores, and imitation learning
sections.summary: Real-world tests showed a median positional repeatability of 1.65 mm and video latency of 137 ms. Complex household chores like operating a dishwasher were teleoperated successfully, and autonomous picking with ACT reached an 80% success rate.
sections.details:
### VI-A Repeatability and Trajectory Tracking
In a 10-cycle repeatability test traversing four target checkpoints from home, the end-effector achieved a median repeatability of $1.65\text{ mm}$ (best case $0.46\text{ mm}$). The dominant error source was torso joint deflection (0.56 mm RMS). In spatial spiral tracking tests, enabling gravity compensation dramatically dropped tracking error from $194\text{ mm}$ to $45\text{ mm}$.

### VI-B Wheel Odometry Accuracy
Dead-reckoning odometry from the 3-wheel swerve encoders was compared against Visual-SLAM from the head ZED camera. Over a 5.72 m trajectory, position error was just $13.5\text{ mm}$ RMS with an orientation error of $1.63^\circ$, confirming centimeter-level precision suitable for smooth teleoperated navigation.

### VI-C Teleoperation Video Latency
Glass-to-glass latency was measured by recording a millisecond stopwatch displayed on a screen through the robot head camera until rendered inside the headset. Direct Wi-Fi hotspot connection yielded an ultra-low latency of $137 \pm 5\text{ ms}$. Camera exposure and readout accounted for the bulk (101–108 ms), while actual network transmission took only $25\text{ ms}$.

### VI-D Real-World Tasks and Imitation Learning
During teleoperation trials, the robot continuously executed tasks demanding whole-body coordination: wiping tables, opening refrigerators, retrieving items from high shelves, carrying laundry baskets with two arms, and pushing dishwasher racks and closing doors (Figure F6).
For imitation learning, 117 demonstrations (totaling 38 minutes) were collected for a multi-fingered pick-and-place task on a plate. In 10 autonomous trials with randomized object positions, the ACT policy succeeded in 8 trials (80%), confirming the real-world efficacy of the end-to-end pipeline.

captions.F6: Sequential photographs of teleoperated real-world tasks. (a) Table wiping, (b) opening a refrigerator, (c) high-shelf retrieval, (d) bimanual basket carrying, and (e) closing a dishwasher door. (f) shows compliant behavior yielding safely when an operator pushes the arms or torso.
captions.F8: Hardware precision evaluations. (a) Dispersion ellipses across four target poses, (b) joint contributions to overall error (torso being largest), (c) fingertip repeatability (median 1.65 mm), and (d, e) tracking error profiles during 3D spatial trajectory following.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: lift speed bottlenecks and broader autonomy
sections.summary: While the standing-desk lift offers affordable vertical reach, its slow speed remains a bottleneck. Future work aims to introduce articulated leg or hip joints and incorporate autonomous planning for long-horizon behaviors.
sections.details:
Despite MABEL's compelling cost-performance balance, several trade-offs remain.

First, while the commercial lift column offers vast vertical travel at low cost, its vertical travel speed is slow. Future designs could replace the column with articulated hip, knee, and ankle joints to achieve faster and more natural crouching and standing dynamics.

Second, the link proportions of the baseline OpenArm do not perfectly match human skeletal geometry. Adapting the arms toward more human-like proportions would further improve reaching ergonomics and retargeting fidelity.

Third, current autonomous learning demonstrations focused primarily on stationary upper-body manipulation. Expanding to mobile manipulation policies over long horizons with onboard LiDAR and SLAM, as well as integrating high-level task planners like Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models, represents a key next step.

sections.heading: Conclusion: an open robotics platform grown by the research community
sections.summary: MABEL delivers advanced whole-body mobility, dexterity, and learning pipelines at one-tenth commercial prices. Just as Linux laid the foundation for open operating systems, MABEL aims to serve as a shared open standard for robot learning.
sections.details:
MABEL unites whole-body mobility, vast reach, active perception, multi-fingered dexterity, and contact compliance at an accessible price point of roughly $8,100. All design files—including CAD models, firmware, ROS 2 stacks, simulation assets, teleoperation software, and learning scripts—are open-sourced.

Just as Linux flourished through global community contributions into foundational software, MABEL is envisioned as a shared, continuously evolving open standard platform for robotics researchers worldwide.

takeaways: Demonstrated that a 56-DOF whole-body mobile bimanual robot can be built and operated for roughly $8,100—about one-tenth the cost of commercial alternatives.
Sparse tracking from the Apple Vision Pro (head and hands only) is sufficient to intuitively drive all 56 DOFs using smart kinematic decoupling (e.g., comfort-box separation for leaning vs. walking).
Sharing the exact same whole-body controller and command interface across teleoperation, simulation, and policy deployment minimizes friction from data collection to ACT policy rollouts.
Quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators coupled with accurate gravity and friction compensation enable safe, compliant physical contact even on budget-conscious hardware.
limitations: The commercial standing-desk lift column provides extensive vertical travel but suffers from slow transit speeds, limiting dynamic whole-body motions.
The 3-wheel swerve base is compact and affordable, but its smaller support polygon compared to 4-wheel setups requires software-based acceleration limits when the lift is raised.
Real-robot imitation learning (ACT) was validated on upper-body pick-and-place tasks; end-to-end autonomous learning that combines continuous mobile base driving remains future work.
